ev.jpn_fc_miyamairi.ujigami.ok: Grandmother carried you herself, wrapped in the best kimono. At the shrine gate you howled at the top of your lungs — and everyone was pleased: the god had heard you and would remember.
ev.jpn_fc_miyamairi.hachiman.ok: Two days on the road, generous offerings — and a priest in a tall cap waved a wand of paper streamers over you. Grandmother grumbled the whole way, but she hung the shrine's amulet round your neck herself.
ev.jpn_fc_miyamairi.later.ok: It is bitterly cold, and an icy wind is no place for a baby. They decided to go when the weather turns; meanwhile grandmother bows towards the shrine every morning.
ev.jpn_fc_miyamairi.title: First visit to the god
ev.jpn_fc_miyamairi.text: You are a month old — time to carry you to the shrine and show you to the guardian god, so that he will know you as his own. Grandmother won't hear of anyone but the local ujigami, the kami who watches over your district. Your father dreams of the great Hachiman shrine: a long road and costly offerings, but the god is mighty and loves warriors.
ev.jpn_fc_miyamairi.note: Miyamairi is a baby's first visit to the shrine of the guardian kami (ujigami), about a month after birth. From that day the child counts as one of the shrine's own people — an ujiko. Hachiman, god of war and patron of warrior houses, had shrines all over the country from the Kamakura period on.
ev.jpn_fc_miyamairi_matsuri.title: The shrine festival
ev.jpn_fc_miyamairi_matsuri.text: At the autumn festival of the shrine where you were carried as a baby, the elders chose you to walk at the head of the procession with a lantern. "One of ours — the god has known this one since swaddling," said the headman. You walked before the god's palanquin with the whole district watching.
ev.jpn_fc_miyamairi_omamori.title: Hachiman's amulet
ev.jpn_fc_miyamairi_omamori.text: Robbers stepped out onto the mountain road, and you, gripping the Hachiman amulet in your fist, shouted so fiercely that they faltered — long enough for other travellers to come up. The little amulet bag is worn through, but you never take it off: the god of warriors seems to remember who was shown to him.
ev.jpn_fc_meigen.veteran.ok: The old man plucked the string till dawn without missing a beat. Leaving, he told your father: "I'll keep this bow — for the child."
ev.jpn_fc_meigen.lord: A man from the lord's house
ev.jpn_fc_meigen.lord.ok: The archer came from your lord's house, and by morning the whole estate knew of your birth. The return gift — silk and a sword — cost dearly, but your father is pleased.
ev.jpn_fc_meigen.monks.ok: The monks chanted till morning amid curling incense, and you slept to their steady voices more soundly than you ever would again.
ev.jpn_fc_meigen.title: The twang of the bowstring
ev.jpn_fc_meigen.text: In a warrior's house a birth is greeted by the bowstring: an archer stands at the door and plucks an empty string, and its hum drives evil spirits from the cradle. Your father must decide whom to trust with the bow — an old kinsman who has seen many battles, or a man from your lord's own house, a great honour that must be repaid with a generous gift. Or instead of the bow, monks could chant sutras all night.
ev.jpn_fc_meigen.note: Meigen, "the sounding bowstring", was a rite against evil spirits performed at births in the imperial palace and in noble warrior houses. An archer plucked a string without an arrow again and again; the Azuma kagami, the chronicle of the Kamakura shoguns, records it at the births of their children.
ev.jpn_fc_meigen_bow.title: The old man's bow
ev.jpn_fc_meigen_bow.text: The old kinsman who once plucked the string by your cradle brought that very bow — cut down to your size. "I promised," he grumbled, and until autumn he stood you before a target in the yard every day. Your arms ached, but by the first frosts you could hit the straw ring from twenty paces.
ev.jpn_fc_meigen_lord.title: The lord's house remembers
ev.jpn_fc_meigen_lord.text: At your lord's house they knew you by name: "We plucked the bowstring for this one." One of the senior retainers took you under their protection — now you have someone whose word carries weight in the lord's hall.
